answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1934–1992 · American poet, essayist & civil rights activist
answer.sourceLine: Lorde wrote this in A Burst of Light (Firebrand Books, 1988), in the book’s epilogue, written as she lived with breast cancer that had spread to her liver. The words are hers verbatim — but the sentence does not stop where the internet stops it. In full: “Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.” Wikiquote carries the line with a full citation to p. 125, in the journal “A Burst of Light: Living with Cancer.”

source.excerpt: Overextending myself is not stretching myself. … Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.
trail: Wikiquote’s Audre Lorde page carries the line with a full citation — the page has no Misattributed or Disputed section — giving the full sentence and citing A Burst of Light: Living with Cancer (1988), p. 125, Firebrand Books, ISBN 0932379400.
Sara Ahmed opens “Selfcare as Warfare” (2014) with the full sentence, attributes it to the epilogue of A Burst of Light, and notes Lorde wrote it while learning she had liver cancer.

The Internet Archive and Open Library catalog records both confirm the edition Wikiquote cites: Firebrand Books, Ithaca, N.Y., 1988, ISBNs 0932379397 / 0932379400, containing the journal “A Burst of Light: Living with Cancer.” The scan is borrow-only, so the page image was not consulted directly.

Refinery29 quotes the fuller passage — including “Overextending myself is not stretching myself” — from the same 1988 collection, and documents how the line has been stripped of its political meaning.
source.excerptNote: The ellipsis marks intervening lines of Lorde’s journal, which remain in copyright and are not reproduced here in full. The popular quote stops at “self-preservation” — a little over halfway through the sentence — and drops the clause that names it as warfare.

As a work first published in 1988 by an identifiable author and publisher, it is in copyright in the United States; rights rest with Audre Lorde’s estate and her publishers. The collection was reissued as A Burst of Light and Other Essays by Dover Publications in 2017 — the year per the Open Library edition record (Ixia Press, Dover’s imprint; ISBN 9780486818993), since the Dover store page itself gives no date. The sentence is quoted here briefly for identification and commentary.

author.bio: Audre Lorde was an American writer, professor, poet and civil rights activist whose work refused to separate her identities as a Black woman, a lesbian, a mother and a feminist. She was diagnosed with breast cancer in 1978; six years later she learned it had metastasized to her liver, and A Burst of Light collects the journal entries she kept while living with it. From 1991 until her death in 1992 she served as New York State Poet Laureate.

misattribution.heading: Right author, half a sentence
misattribution.intro: This one is not a stolen quote — the attribution is correct and the words are Lorde’s exactly. What goes wrong is where the sentence ends. The version in circulation is the front half of a longer thought, and the missing half is the part that carries the politics.

items.why: “Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation” is verbatim Lorde — but her sentence continues, “and that is an act of political warfare.” Wikiquote’s sourced entry gives the whole sentence; Sara Ahmed quotes it in full and stresses that Lorde meant survival under systemic oppression, not the individualism the short form now serves.

A second variant swaps Lorde’s “Caring for myself” for the branded term “self-care” — yielding “Self-care is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation.” PassItOn displays exactly this form, credited to Lorde with no book, no page and no political clause. Lorde did not use the word “self-care” in this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Lorde’s actual sentence, in A Burst of Light (Firebrand Books, 1988), p. 125: “Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.” Per Wikiquote’s fully cited entry.

context.heading: The half that gets cut
lead: Lorde wrote this line in the late 1980s, in a journal she kept as her breast cancer spread to her liver. It is not advice about rest; it is a note-to-self about triage, written by a woman calculating how much of herself she could spend on the world before there was nothing left. The lines just before it are blunt and clipped — “Overextending myself is not stretching myself” — the sound of someone learning a limit the hard way.

That is why the missing clause matters. Lorde did not write that caring for herself was self-preservation and leave it there; she wrote that self-preservation was an act of political warfare — a claim that a Black lesbian woman staying alive under systems built to grind her down is itself a hostile act. Cut the sentence at “self-preservation” and it becomes permission to take a bath. Sara Ahmed calls the line “much loved, much cited” while arguing that Lorde meant survival under oppression, not the wellness-industry individualism it now gets used to sell.
detailsBody: The short form is simply more sellable. “Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation” reads as a tidy, universal permission slip — it fits a mug, a mat, a caption. The full sentence names a fight, and a fight needs an opponent, which is exactly the part a wellness brand cannot print.

A Refinery29 essay quotes the fuller passage and argues that the term self-care “was insidiously co-opted by white people and stripped of its BLACK radical meaning.” With Lorde’s sentence, that stripping happens at the level of punctuation — one dropped clause at a time.
context.pull: The half that gets cut is the half that made it political.
